analysis.one_liner: Lets striking and locked-out workers collect unemployment benefits after two weeks off the job.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 5 total Senate sponsors, was sent to the Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal rules, workers on strike are generally considered employed and most states deny them unemployment benefits, so income stops the day a walkout begins. This bill would change federal law so striking workers can claim unemployment benefits starting 14 days after a strike begins, or immediately if their employer locks them out or hires permanent replacements. It would also waive the usual requirement that claimants be available for other work, since strikers are trying to return to their own jobs. The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearings or votes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on strike or locked out by their employers. Today, a strike can mean months with no paycheck, which pressures workers into accepting contract terms or abandoning the strike. Benefits starting two weeks in, or right away for lockouts and permanent replacements, would let workers hold out longer without losing their homes or going into debt. Workers who lose their jobs as an indirect result of a labor dispute would also qualify.

how_it_helps.text: Makes unemployment compensation payable to workers 'unable to work due to a labor dispute' beginning 14 days after a strike starts, the day a lockout begins, the day the employer hires permanent replacements, or the day the strike ends, whichever comes first [S2].
Exempts striking workers from the Social Security Act requirement that UI claimants be available for work, so they can collect while waiting to return to their own jobs [S2].
Covers workers idled as an indirect result of a labor dispute, such as workers at other plants laid off because a supplier's strike stopped production [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The unemployment insurance system, which is funded by payroll taxes on employers. Benefits to strikers would draw down state and federal UI trust funds, meaning higher UI tax costs for employers over time and, ultimately, some pass-through to prices. Employers facing strikes would also bear more leverage in negotiations, since workers could hold out longer on benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and the unemployment insurance system

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new group of claimants to a system funded by employer payroll taxes, raising UI costs for businesses, especially those with unionized workforces, and straining trust funds during major strikes [S2].

Critics of paying strike benefits argue it puts public money behind one side of a private labor negotiation and could lengthen disputes by making a strike cheaper for workers to sustain; federal law currently leaves this choice to the states, and most states deny benefits to strikers [S2].
The bill does not include a new funding source, so the cost would fall on the existing UI financing structure rather than a dedicated account [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill addresses a real hardship: strikes now often last months, and workers currently go unpaid throughout. The cost is real too — it expands a payroll-tax-financed system at employers' expense and could make strikes longer and more common. Whether that is a flaw or the point depends on whose side of the bargaining table you sit; the design is simple and does not attempt to offset the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Schiff introduced the bill on September 8, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S4].
The bill has 4 cosponsors (3 Democrats, 1 Independent) in addition to its Democratic sponsor [S3].

The bill would amend federal tax and Social Security Act provisions so that workers unable to work because of a labor dispute can receive unemployment compensation, starting 14 days into a strike or immediately upon a lockout or the hiring of permanent replacements [S2].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history since the September 8 referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Striking workers remain in the same position as before: no unemployment benefits in most states. Employers facing strikes are better off that the bill has not moved, since the current rule — unpaid strikers pressured to settle — remains intact.

for.name: Sen. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Empowering Striking Workers Act of 2025 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: 4 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill after introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 8, 2025 and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — while Congress remains in session.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 Senate supporters are Democrats or Independents; no Republican cosponsors appear in the record, and the bill has not been scheduled for any committee action.

industries.note: The bill would make strikes materially cheaper for workers to sustain, shifting bargaining leverage toward labor and raising the cost of breaking a strike with permanent replacements. Employers' interest in this bill runs against the workers it would support.

industries.industry: Unemployment insurance system (state and federal trust funds funded by employer payroll taxes)
industries.note: Paying benefits to strikers would draw on a system financed by employer payroll taxes, expanding costs during large labor disputes with no dedicated funding in the bill.
Strikes are unions' main bargaining weapon; benefits after two weeks would let members hold out for better contract terms, and the bill covers representation disputes as well as wage disputes.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Finance Committee with only 5 sponsors and no Republican support rarely reach the floor. Unless cosponsorship broadens substantially or labor issues force it onto the agenda, the likely path is no action before the 119th Congress ends, making this a position-taking bill unless it gains real momentum.
